key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders set autopay only slightly above the minimum and reduced manual payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live UK credit card accounts with a 6-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly shows a default-style nudge can shift a nominal enrollment/behavior metric without changing the real financial outcome — exactly the vanity-enrollment risk the support team raised for round-up defaults, and unlike most of this literature it studies a genuine consumer financial product rather than an employer plan.
limitations: credit card debt repayment, not a savings product
the mechanism is shrouding a minimum-payment option, not an enrollment default per se
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-product evidence that a default-style nudge can raise a compliance metric without improving the substantive outcome, directly bearing on the brief's central 'vanity enrollment' question.

key_finding: Synthesizes plan-design literature showing automatic enrollment and default investment options raise participation but can produce longer-term participant disengagement.
methodology: Narrative literature review, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives an up-to-date synthesis of the disengagement-cost side of defaults that the support team worries about, but is scoped entirely to employer DC retirement plans, not a consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given in the abstract
synthesis rather than primary evidence
relevance_reason: Background synthesis of the closest analogous (employer) literature on default disengagement, useful context but off the brief's setting.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity — low contribution rates, inactive account management, and account churn.
methodology: Narrative/policy commentary article, abstract-only, no new primary data.
why_it_matters: Restates the disengagement concern the support team already raises, but adds no new evidence beyond papers already better documented elsewhere in this set.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not consumer savings
zero citations and no data behind the claims
purely narrative, no effect sizes
relevance_reason: Echoes but does not add evidence to the passivity/disengagement concern already better supported by other shortlisted papers.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual review and research-agenda paper synthesizing prior default-effect literature, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides the conceptual vocabulary for the exact question the team needs answered — whether the round-up default's effect on enrollment will persist or decay, and for whom — framed at the level of general consumer decision-making rather than employer plans.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not new empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Supplies the general framework for predicting persistence and heterogeneity of default effects that the brief's core trade-off depends on.

key_finding: Random assignment to Medicare Part D default plans shows default enrollment has large, persistent effects on drug plan enrollment and utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even to substantial losses from the default.
methodology: Three natural/randomized experiments using Medicare administrative data.
why_it_matters: Shows a default effect can persist strongly even when it costs the passively-enrolled person — a caution against assuming persistence implies the default is benign — but the setting is health-insurance enrollment, not a savings feature.
limitations: Medicare health-insurance enrollment, not consumer financial savings
beneficiaries are typically elderly/low-income, unlike a general banking-app population
relevance_reason: Strong causal evidence on default persistence and active-choice attentiveness, useful by analogy despite an off-domain setting.

key_finding: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans finds automatic enrollment raises steady-state saving rates by only 0.6% of income and auto-escalation defaults by only 0.3%, and only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on the first date, with more opting out later.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation and balance-withdrawal dynamics.
why_it_matters: The strongest recent quantitative evidence that headline default 'take-up' overstates the real medium/long-run effect on amounts saved — precisely the vanity-enrollment risk the support team raises for round-up defaults.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated auto-escalation, no direct fintech app analogue
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with real numbers on how much smaller the effect is once medium/long-run dynamics are accounted for.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals eventually actively opt out; the default effect is stronger when incentives are higher and knowledge of enrollment status is lower.
methodology: Administrative and survey data linked around a nationwide policy introduction.
why_it_matters: Adds a large, explicit effect-size estimate for a default versus opt-out design, and shows the effect depends on incentive salience and awareness, but in a public pension rather than consumer-app setting.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a self-directed consumer product
most individuals eventually opt out, limiting persistence
relevance_reason: A large, explicit default effect-size estimate with heterogeneity by incentive and knowledge, though in an off-domain public pension context.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions at 12 months attenuates substantially by 36 months, though it still reduces inequality in savings; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250, smaller than prior estimates.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives the clearest horizon-by-horizon evidence of how a default's apparent enrollment win decays over time, directly bearing on whether the round-up default effect will hold at 6-12 months, even though measured in an employer 401(k) setting.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not a consumer round-up feature
switching-cost estimate is model-derived, not directly observed
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of how default effects attenuate over medium-run horizons, the exact persistence question the brief asks about.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower consumers' rating of the advice delivered, especially when the default is one they refuse.
methodology: Three experiments; the largest uses representative samples across five European countries.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the reputational/manipulation cost of a default in a European consumer financial-advice context — exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry design decision — and shows framing of the default question itself changes outcomes.
limitations: wealth-management risk allocation, not a round-up savings multiplier
no long-term follow-up on retention or amount saved
relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial evidence, with effect sizes, on when a default is perceived as manipulative rather than helpful — central to the brief's dark-pattern concern.

key_finding: Employees under automatic 401(k) enrollment reach over 85% participation, but about 80% initially anchor at the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, and half remain at the default rate/fund even after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that people anchor on preset default levels rather than actively choosing — the mechanism behind the brief's concern that a pre-set multiplier could suppress higher contributions — but from the classic, pre-app, employer-plan era the brief says to weight less.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans from an earlier era, not a consumer fintech app
undated working paper, superseded empirically by more recent studies in this set
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for anchoring on default levels, the phenomenon the brief worries about for the round-up multiplier, from the classic literature the brief explicitly deprioritizes.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together; adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20-30% menu would capture 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the 'level' decision: it models how a preset menu of numeric options anchors chosen amounts and what changing the menu does to welfare versus revenue — the same structural question as choosing which round-up multiplier to preset and whether to add more options.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
US taxi setting, not an EU banking app
relevance_reason: Closest available structural analysis of how a preset numeric menu anchors consumer choice and what changing the menu does to welfare, directly transferable to the round-up multiplier design decision.

key_finding: In an opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings program at five UK firms, no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among those observed over 12 months, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution at month 12.
methodology: Administrative panel data on payroll-deduction short-term savings account activation and use at five UK firms.
why_it_matters: The closest product analogue to a round-up savings pot (liquid, withdrawable, small, automatic) shows opt-in produces very low take-up but high persistence among those enrolled — direct evidence for the entry-design trade-off between reach and engagement.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel, not a direct-to-consumer banking app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice conditions in this study
relevance_reason: Uniquely close product analogue (liquid short-term savings, UK) giving real opt-in take-up and 12-month persistence numbers directly relevant to the entry decision.

key_finding: Provides a general characterization of when opt-out-minimizing versus opt-out-maximizing default rules are optimal; under designer-chooser agreement on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, verified via numerical simulation.
methodology: Theoretical/computational model of optimal default design with asymptotic approximations validated by simulation.
why_it_matters: Gives a principled framework for deciding whether to default users in or out at all, rather than relying only on the raw enrollment-lift argument — directly relevant to resolving the internal debate about whether to default everyone into round-up saving.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical estimates for a savings-app setting
abstract does not specify a financial or consumer-app application
relevance_reason: Only paper offering a normative theory of when defaulting users in versus minimizing opt-outs is actually optimal, speaking directly to the entry-design decision at stake.

key_finding: Provides a taxonomy of six categories of autonomy violations under EU law that determine when a default-based choice architecture crosses into a regulated 'dark pattern.'
methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis mapping EU consumer-protection law and building a normative taxonomy; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the framework for judging whether an opt-out entry design in the EU would read as manipulative rather than helpful, directly bearing on the legal/reputational risk named in the brief.
limitations: Legal/doctrinal analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or engagement effects
Not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly names when a default is legally/normatively a dark pattern in the EU, the reputational risk the brief flags for the entry decision.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees remained un-opted-out at 12 months (vs ~50% opt-out in plans with lower defaults), and many stayed below the rate that would maximize their employer match.
methodology: Analysis of employer retirement-plan enrollment data with an unusually high 12% default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans; abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Shows a strong preset level anchors people at a suboptimal contribution point, informing the risk that a high preset round-up multiplier could anchor users away from a better-fitting level, though in an employer-plan context.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed banking product
No explanation of how the employer-intermediary mechanism differs from a fintech app
relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence on anchoring to a high default level, relevant by analogy to the multiplier default decision.

key_finding: Abstract text is unavailable ('Trant'); the title indicates four large UK field experiments automating short-term payroll savings, but no extractable findings are given.
methodology: Field experiments (four large UK studies) on automating short-term payroll savings; abstract-only, content unusable.
why_it_matters: Potentially close evidence on automating short-term, liquid savings enrolment by leading default-effect researchers, but the abstract provides nothing concrete to act on here.
limitations: Abstract text is missing/garbled, so no verifiable findings can be cited
Payroll-based savings mechanism differs from a self-directed banking app feature
relevance_reason: Title suggests directly relevant short-term savings automation evidence from top researchers, but the abstract content is unusable for scoring.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into just-in-time SMS overdraft alerts at major UK banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though users still captured less than half of the achievable savings.
methodology: At-scale randomized field experiments run with major UK retail banks on an existing consumer banking app feature.
why_it_matters: This is the closest available evidence to our own decision: automatic enrolment into a consumer banking app feature with quantified effect sizes, plus evidence that even a successful default leaves much of the potential benefit unrealized, directly bearing on enrolment vs. amount-saved.
limitations: Overdraft alerts, not a savings/contribution feature, so 'amount saved' logic differs from round-up mechanics
No 6-12 month persistence data given beyond the trial window
relevance_reason: Closest prior work: consumer retail-bank automatic-enrolment field experiments with quantified effect sizes in the exact UK/EU regulatory and market context.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increased savings (£32-38/month) but was partially offset by increased unsecured debt (£7/month) and higher mortgage take-up over 41 months, though credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Randomized roll-out of UK automatic-enrollment pensions across ~160,000 small employers, with 41-month panel data on debt and savings.
why_it_matters: Shows default-driven saving gains can be partly offset elsewhere in household finances over the medium term, a caution against treating higher enrolment or contributions as a clean welfare gain, though in an employer-pension setting.
limitations: Employer-sponsored pension context, not a self-directed consumer banking feature
Offsetting-debt mechanism may not scale down to small, liquid round-up sums
relevance_reason: Long-run distributional evidence that default-driven saving can have offsetting financial effects, informing whether default effects represent real welfare gains.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (extra step) to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged individuals.
methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal/addition of an auto-enrollment step in a public health-insurance selection market, with a theoretical adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction (moving away from opt-out toward active choice/opt-in) has large, distributionally uneven effects on who stays enrolled, directly bearing on who is helped versus hurt by our entry-design choice.
limitations: Health-insurance selection market, not a consumer financial savings product
Adverse-selection framing does not map cleanly onto a savings feature with no insurance risk pooling
relevance_reason: Strongest available distributional evidence on the enrolment cost of adding friction, bearing directly on who is hurt by moving away from opt-out.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with disproportionately larger effects on smaller, first-time donors who likely did not intend the recurring commitment.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the different timing of default rollout across political-campaign donation websites.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the support team's concern in a real setting: defaults on recurring financial commitments raise uptake but generate disproportionate refunds/complaints among naive users, the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk named in the brief.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings or banking product
No 6-12 month retention data beyond refund requests
relevance_reason: Closest empirical demonstration of a default-induced recurring financial commitment causing complaint/refund behavior concentrated among less-experienced users, mirroring the support team's objection.

key_finding: A default option raises the reference point for search, improving realized choice quality, while those who reject the default self-select into more effective search and find higher-ranked options.
methodology: Theoretical search model with reference-dependent utility, tested with lab experiments.
why_it_matters: General mechanism for how defaults interact with active search/choice, but too abstract and generic to inform the specific enrolment or multiplier-level decisions we face.
limitations: Lab experiment with an abstract search task, no financial or savings context
No enrollment or contribution-level analogue
relevance_reason: Background theory on default/reference effects in choice, but not decision-changing for this brief.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage was 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months.
methodology: Difference-in-differences quasi-experiment exploiting the staggered rollout of EU-mandated choice screens across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Provides rare 15-month persistence evidence on a real EU-regulated active-choice intervention altering default-driven behavior at scale, directly informing whether active choice produces durable change rather than a one-off signup blip.
limitations: Mobile browser default setting, not a financial or savings product
Underlying mechanism (search/browser preference) differs from a savings-contribution decision
relevance_reason: Closest available large-scale, long-horizon evidence on active-choice mandates changing default-driven behavior in the exact EU regulatory context the brief operates in.

key_finding: Generalizable opt-out interface designs (applying one choice across many sites/categories) increased opt-out efficiency and reduced disruption without using defaults; the least-disruptive scheme left 98% of participants feeling undisrupted.
methodology: Usability study of nine privacy-choice interface schemes implemented in a browser extension, tested with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Offers interface-design ideas for non-default active-choice mechanisms, tangential to the round-up feature's onboarding UI but focused on a different (privacy) domain.
limitations: Privacy opt-out context (data sharing), not financial enrolment or savings
No enrolment-rate or amount-saved outcomes reported
relevance_reason: Marginal relevance as a UI-design precedent for active choice without defaults, but off-topic domain.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-ups, but effortful downstream completion (exam participation and passing) improved only for previously 'responsive' students, with no effect for non-responsive individuals.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults to opt-out at a university, tracking downstream effortful task completion.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the mechanism the support team worries about: a default can inflate nominal sign-up while doing nothing for engagement among people who were not going to act anyway, precisely the 'vanity enrollment' risk for round-up savings.
limitations: University exam sign-up, not a financial savings decision
No amount-saved or 6-12 month withdrawal data given
relevance_reason: Best available evidence that opt-out defaults can inflate nominal participation without changing effortful downstream behavior for disengaged users, the core mechanism behind the brief's vanity-enrolment worry.

key_finding: After the Pension Protection Act made target-date funds a default, stock allocation became age-dependent per the TDF glidepath, while contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the PPA policy change as a natural experiment.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults strongly shift the specific dimension they target (allocation) while leaving an unrelated behavior (contribution rate) largely unchanged, a caution that a preset multiplier default may anchor the multiplier without changing the underlying saving amount.
limitations: Employer retirement-plan investment defaults, not a consumer savings enrolment/level decision
The contribution-rate finding is incidental to the paper's main focus on portfolio allocation
relevance_reason: Long-run evidence that defaults reshape the dimension they target while other behaviors stay flat, informing the anchoring question.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested nudges -including default options- significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to a control group, with the largest backfire effects from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions in China.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise underlying the internal argument for opt-out enrolment, showing defaults can backfire and reduce stated willingness to contribute in some cultural/institutional contexts.
limitations: Small online-survey RCT (n=220) measuring stated willingness, not real enrolment behavior
Chinese voluntary-pension context, culturally and institutionally distant from an EU banking app
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the shortlist that default options can backfire and reduce contribution intentions, directly against the brief's internal argument for defaulting everyone in.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians rating 36 hypothetical financial interventions, people rated most interventions positively and preferred System-2 (deliberative) interventions and saving-framed messages, with transparency having no significant effect on approval.
methodology: Pre-registered between/within-subjects survey experiment varying transparency, framing and System-1/System-2 targeting; six outcome measures including manipulation perception; representative Australian sample.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial nudge is read as helpful versus manipulative, which is exactly the reputational risk question the EU consumer-protection framing raises about defaulting people into round-up savings.
limitations: hypothetical vignette scenarios rather than a live product decision
does not measure actual enrolment or savings behaviour, only stated approval
relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer-facing evidence on manipulation perception of financial nudges, the closest available evidence to the brief's dark-pattern concern.

key_finding: Offering cash-transfer recipients a bank-account delivery choice had no average effect on savings, but raised balances for those who previously held nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment on conditional cash transfer beneficiaries in a developing-country banking context, comparing cash versus account delivery.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults/choice architecture around account-based saving may only move people who were previously unsaved, echoing the brief's concern that lifts could be concentrated on already-marginal segments.
limitations: developing-country CCT population, not a consumer fintech app
not an opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment design
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence on heterogeneous response to account-based saving mechanisms, weak fit to the specific enrolment-default question.

key_finding: Abstract fragment describes a universal automatic IRA with an emergency (liquid) savings component, but gives no usable comparative data.
methodology: abstract-only; abstract text is truncated and largely uninterpretable.
why_it_matters: A universal (non-employer) auto-enrolled savings vehicle with a liquid component is structurally closer to our round-up feature than a 401(k), but the abstract provides no extractable finding to act on.
limitations: abstract is garbled/truncated with no interpretable results
unclear enrolment mechanism or effect size
relevance_reason: Setting (universal, non-employer auto-enrolment savings) is close to ours, but content offers no usable evidence.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation ('default' behaviour).
methodology: Before/after administrative data analysis at a single large U.S. corporation comparing opt-in versus automatic-enrolment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults anchor both participation and the chosen level, the empirical basis for the internal 'defaults lift enrolment' argument our team is testing.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
single-firm case study
no distributional or manipulation analysis
relevance_reason: Classic foundational result on default enrolment and anchoring that the later literature (including our other candidates) builds on and argues with.

key_finding: Title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrolment in a defined-contribution plan; no abstract content available.
methodology: abstract-only; no abstract text provided.
why_it_matters: On-topic by title but unusable without content; cannot inform any specific decision as presented.
limitations: no abstract available to extract findings
employer DC plan setting
relevance_reason: Topically relevant title but no substantive content to evaluate.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status are both associated with under-saving for retirement and with early withdrawal once a withdrawal option opens, a 'double jeopardy' pattern.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension-reform introducing early withdrawal.
why_it_matters: Directly bears on who is helped versus hurt by a savings feature: it suggests low-trust and minority users are more likely to disengage and withdraw, which is exactly the support team's disengagement concern, though in a mandatory pension rather than a consumer app.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a self-directed consumer savings product
withdrawal decision studied is a one-off policy-driven event, not routine round-up withdrawal
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on disengagement/withdrawal risk by trust and demographic group, relevant to the brief's 'who is hurt' question, though in an off-domain pension setting.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on being automatically enrolled in a booster-vaccination default reduced their stated intention to comply and reduced approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment policy.
why_it_matters: Shows that making a default salient to the person it affects can backfire, directly relevant to whether disclosing an opt-out round-up default (as EU consumer law requires) could itself trigger disengagement or complaints.
limitations: vaccination policy context, not a financial product
measures stated intentions, not actual enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: Contradicts the simple 'defaults always help' premise by showing reflection on a default can reduce compliance and approval, an analogous backlash mechanism to the brief's manipulation concern.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment and employer matching contributions are associated with higher retirement-plan participation among U.S. Millennials, while their absence is linked to non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Correlational confirmation of the default-enrolment participation lift already well established by stronger prior evidence; adds little new to the decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored plan, not a consumer app
correlational, not causal
no persistence or amount-saved data
relevance_reason: Redundant confirmation of a well-established effect in an employer-plan setting with weaker (correlational) evidence than other candidates.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) retirement contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induced mostly asset-shifting (each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only 1 cent); ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by automatic contributions, and active savers are wealthier and more sophisticated.
methodology: Population-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish savings and retirement account activity.
why_it_matters: The strongest available quantification of how much more effective passive/automatic mechanisms are than active-choice incentives, and of who the passive-responders are, directly informing the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question and the credibility of the defaults-lift-enrolment premise.
limitations: Danish retirement/pension accounts, employer-linked, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
subsidy-based active choice differs from an active-choice onboarding screen
relevance_reason: Closest and strongest available evidence quantifying the size and distributional heterogeneity of default versus active-choice effects on saving, a necessary reference point even though the setting is retirement accounts.

key_finding: Active-choice policies (requiring an explicit yes/no) are an effective alternative to opt-out defaults where opt-out is infeasible or unethical, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option outperforms plain active choice in field experiments.
methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against no-default and opt-out conditions.
why_it_matters: The closest existing evidence directly comparing active choice against opt-out defaults, the central question behind the brief's decision on whether forced choice can capture most of the enrolment benefit without the disengagement cost.
limitations: applications drawn mainly from health/medication adherence and retirement contexts, not a fintech app
abstract gives no numeric enrolment effect sizes
relevance_reason: Directly targets the active-choice-versus-default comparison (C6) that decision 1 turns on, proposing a specific enhanced design the team could test.

key_finding: A synthesis of household-finance behaviour covering consumption/saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and of interventions (education, peer effects, product design, choice architecture, disclosure) that firms and governments use to shape financial outcomes.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter synthesizing empirical and behavioural-economics findings across household finance topics.
why_it_matters: Gives the broad synthesis and vocabulary of choice-architecture and product-design interventions in household finance the brief needs as a review-level reference, spanning beyond the employer-retirement literature to consumer product design generally.
limitations: broad overview rather than a focused effect-size estimate on round-up savings defaults
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
relevance_reason: Serves the portfolio's need for a synthesis/review of the choice-architecture literature across consumer financial products, not only employer retirement plans.

key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic enrolment raised 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the default savings rate (2-3%) and default fund, and half still remained at the default rate and fund after three years; automatic enrolment increased saving mainly in the lower tail of the distribution.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrolment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative evidence that a pre-set contribution level anchors most people for years, directly bearing on decision 2 (whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor users away from a higher level they might otherwise choose) and on whether the enrolment lift is a net saving-amount gain or just a nominal one.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) setting rather than a self-directed consumer app
three-firm sample, U.S. retirement context
relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence on anchoring at a pre-set default level and its persistence over years, central to the level/multiplier decision.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to a salary-linked savings account with default enrolment increased participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% matching incentive), driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios; default assignment also increased favourable attitudes toward saving and made people more likely to actively choose to save after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with multiple treatment arms isolating mechanisms behind default effects, on employees in Afghanistan.
why_it_matters: The strongest causal evidence available on why defaults change behaviour and whether the effect is 'real' engagement or mere inertia, since it shows attitudes and later active choices shifted too, directly bearing on the support team's concern that default-enrolled users are only nominally, not genuinely, engaged.
limitations: salary-linked account tied to employment, not a self-directed banking-app sign-up
developing-country labour-market context, not the EU consumer setting
relevance_reason: Provides the clearest experimental evidence and mechanism for why defaults work and whether the effect persists into genuine engagement, the strongest available causal estimate in the batch.

key_finding: A randomized reminder-nudge intervention in a consumer credit card app cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment (RCT) with a financial management platform in Brazil, comparing users randomized to receive payment reminders versus not, tracking downstream fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Gives a quantified, real consumer-fintech demonstration that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — directly bears on the brief's requirement to check who is hurt, not just average enrolment lift, before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
